sections.heading: How to Apply for PSARA License Registration Online in 2026: Step-by-Step Guide
paragraphs: Setting up a security agency takes more than just hiring guards or picking up clients. The law is clear: under the Private Security Agencies (Regulation) Act, 2005, you can’t provide private security services until you get a PSARA license. These days, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has made things simpler by moving the application process online through the Private Security Agency Licensing Portal.
If you’re planning to launch your security business in 2026, it's smart to understand the process up front—trust me, it saves a lot of time, frustration, and unnecessary costs.

Absolutely. The MHA’s Private Security Agency Licensing Portal at psara.gov.in handles PSARA applications digitally. This portal covers everything, including license information by state or union territory (UT).

But don’t expect instant approval—you still need to go through document checks, police verification, and screening by the state or UT’s controlling authority. Under Section 7 of the Act, your application only moves ahead after proper inquiries and a police no-objection certificate.
The central online portal is the Private Security Agency Licensing Portal operated under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

Your controlling authority is the one appointed by your state or UT government, not a central body. That’s because licenses are given for specific districts or states, not the whole country. You can apply for a single district, multiple districts, or the whole state.

And it gets better (or trickier): Each state can have its own checklist and forms. For example, West Bengal’s portal comes with its own set of forms you’ll need to fill out—so don’t just copy documents from somewhere else.

The MHA makes it clear: Indian citizens, partnerships, firms, or companies intending to provide private security should proceed with a PSARA license online apply. But the rules go further—a company must be registered in India, and the proprietor or main partners or directors have to be Indian citizens. Section 6 of the Act also lists situations where someone isn’t eligible.
Before You Start: Check—
That your business entity is legally set up
That the key people (proprietor, partners, directors) meet all eligibility conditions
That your main office is within the area where you want to operate
That you can prove access to the required training for your staff
That all your info will pass background verification
Most people skip this. Don’t. Figure out exactly where you plan to operate—fees (and paperwork) change depending on how many districts or if it’s the whole state.
